pages.title: Selling a House in Christchurch | Piripi & Sons Real Estate
pages.description: Understand the steps of selling a house in Christchurch, from an evidence-based appraisal to marketing, agency agreements and settlement.
pages.intro: Selling property is a sequence of decisions, not just an advertisement. Explore the questions to ask, how an appraisal works and what to confirm before appointing a real estate professional.

sections.heading: Start by understanding your property's position
paragraphs: A useful first discussion covers your reasons for selling, your timeframe, the property type and what you need to achieve. A market appraisal should be based on current comparable evidence and the condition and features of your property, rather than a generic online estimate.
Ask what assumptions were used and whether the proposed sale method suits your circumstances.

sections.heading: Compare selling methods and marketing plans
paragraphs: Auction, deadline sale, tender and advertised-price methods each involve trade-offs. Ask how interested buyers will be reached, what marketing is recommended, who pays for it and how the asking strategy could change if buyer feedback differs from expectations.
bullets: Request an itemised estimate of marketing and commission, including GST treatment.
Ask who will handle enquiries, viewings, offers and negotiations.
Read the agency agreement carefully and take independent legal advice.

sections.heading: When you're ready to talk
paragraphs: Piripi & Sons welcomes preliminary property enquiries. Corrie is Christchurch-based. The scope of any representation, service area, appraisal and agency arrangements must be confirmed before an engagement begins.
If you are based overseas, see the separate international information page, where purchase eligibility and out-of-area arrangements are treated as case-by-case questions.

pages.title: Christchurch Property Appraisals | Piripi & Sons
pages.description: Learn what a written property appraisal involves in New Zealand and ask about an initial Christchurch property appraisal conversation.
pages.intro: A professional property appraisal is a reasoned assessment of an expected selling price at a particular time. It is not a guaranteed sale price or an automated valuation.

sections.heading: What should a property appraisal include?
paragraphs: Under New Zealand's professional conduct rules, a written appraisal must realistically reflect current market conditions and, where available, be supported by comparable sales of similar properties. If there are no meaningful comparable sales, that limitation must be explained.

A conversation about an appraisal may consider your property's size, condition, location, improvements and current comparable evidence. Any actual assessment and representation must be provided through the appropriate licensed agency arrangements.
bullets: Information about the property and any major alterations.
Recent comparable property sales and relevant market conditions.
A clear explanation of how an estimated range was reached.

sections.heading: Appraisal, online estimate and formal valuation
paragraphs: An online estimate can be a broad automated indication, but it does not replace a property-specific written appraisal. A registered valuation is a different professional service, often commissioned for lending, legal or other purposes. Ask which document you need before making decisions.
The site does not calculate a value or promise an instant appraisal.

sections.heading: Preparing for the conversation
paragraphs: Have the general property location, style, timeframe and any unusual features ready. There is no need to email identity documents, title deeds or financial records at the enquiry stage.
If you are comparing professionals, ask about the evidence, sale options, proposed marketing plan and agency obligations before signing.

pages.title: Buying a Home in New Zealand | Piripi & Sons
pages.description: Straightforward guidance for New Zealand home buyers: finance, due diligence, sale agreements and questions to ask before making an offer.
pages.h1: Buying a home in New Zealand
pages.intro: Buying a home involves more than finding a property. Understanding finance, investigations, contracts and deadlines helps you make clearer decisions.

sections.heading: Before you start
paragraphs: Determine your budget with a lender or mortgage adviser, including a margin for legal and property investigation costs. Clarify whether your finance is conditional and what evidence your lender will need.
Choose a lawyer or conveyancer early. They can review the sale and purchase agreement and help you understand important conditions before you sign.

refs.label: Settled — independent buyer and seller guidance

sections.heading: Check the property, not just the brochure
paragraphs: Depending on the property, due diligence may include a building inspection, title review, LIM information, insurance availability, rates and any body-corporate or tenancy documents. Appropriate checks vary, so obtain independent professional advice.
A sale and purchase agreement is legally significant. Do not assume a general website guide is sufficient to evaluate the risks in a particular purchase.

sections.heading: Overseas buyers need an eligibility check
paragraphs: Eligibility to buy residential land in New Zealand depends on the buyer's circumstances and the property. Most overseas people cannot simply buy residential property because they have sufficient funds. Certain pathways require consent and detailed legal assessment.

sections.heading: Start with the neighbourhood and property type
paragraphs: A property on the edge of the central city may raise different questions from a hillside property, a new subdivision home or an older character house. Local context can include school zones, transport, surrounding development, flood information and property-specific restrictions.
These factors should be checked through authoritative sources and qualified professionals where relevant. We do not publish invented suburb prices or claim to cover every neighbourhood.

sections.heading: Why property-specific evidence matters
paragraphs: A credible appraisal draws on comparable properties and current market conditions. Differences in floor area, land, building condition, location and sale circumstances may make two nearby houses unlike one another.
If you are thinking of selling in Christchurch, request an explanation of the comparable evidence used and the proposed marketing approach.

pages.title: How to Choose a Real Estate Agent in NZ | Questions to Ask
pages.description: A practical New Zealand checklist: verifying a real estate professional, comparing appraisals, commission and marketing plans.
pages.h1: How to choose a real estate professional
pages.intro: Choosing who to work with can affect your selling experience. Compare the information and service proposed, rather than relying on claims or a single estimated sale price.

sections.heading: Check the licence and who supervises the work
paragraphs: The Real Estate Authority maintains the public register of licensed salespeople, branch managers and agents. The classes are different, and a salesperson acts for or on behalf of a licensed agent.
Check the relevant licensed agency as well as the individual. A polished website is not a substitute for independent verification.

refs.label: REA — choosing a real estate professional

sections.heading: Ask the same questions of each person
paragraphs: Invite more than one professional to assess the property where practical. Ask what comparable sales underpin the appraisal, which sale method is recommended and what is included in the marketing proposal.
bullets: Who will personally manage enquiries and viewings?
What are all commission, marketing and administration costs, with GST clear?
What happens if the marketing strategy needs to change?
How and when can the agency agreement end?

sections.heading: Read everything before signing
paragraphs: An agency agreement creates legal rights and obligations. Obtain and read the REA consumer guide and ask a lawyer to review anything unclear. Written marketing costs, commission estimates and agency terms matter just as much as the appraisal.

pages.title: How to Sell a House in New Zealand | Step-by-Step
pages.description: A concise NZ home-selling sequence: goals, appraisal, agency agreement, marketing, offers, legal review and settlement.
pages.intro: The sequence varies by property and sale method, but a simple checklist helps sellers understand where professional advice and decisions are needed.

sections.heading: 1. Plan before you list
paragraphs: Clarify your timeframe, any buying plans, expected costs and the role of your lawyer or conveyancer. Check whether the property has any known issues or information that needs professional explanation.
A property-specific written appraisal and realistic marketing discussion help you understand options.

sections.heading: 2. Compare proposals and authorise the work
paragraphs: A licensed agency must explain its proposal, provide the required guide and written estimates, and enter an appropriate agency agreement before undertaking the agency work. Review commission, marketing spend, sale method, duration and cancellation rules.

sections.heading: 3. Market, evaluate offers and reach settlement
paragraphs: Marketing activity, buyer feedback, offers and conditions may require decisions and independent legal advice. Once an agreement is reached, finance, due diligence and other conditions must be resolved before settlement obligations are completed.
Ask how updates and offers will be communicated, who negotiates, and when your lawyer should become involved.

pages.title: Costs of Selling a House in NZ | Commission and Marketing
pages.description: Understand New Zealand house-selling costs and questions to ask about real estate commission, advertising, legal work and GST.
pages.h1: What does it cost to sell a house?
pages.intro: The total cost of selling can be more than the agent's commission. Confirm an itemised estimate and seek appropriate advice before signing any agreement.

sections.heading: Common cost categories
paragraphs: Potential costs include agency commission, marketing and photography, legal and conveyancing services, minor repairs or presentation, moving costs and any lending-related adjustments. Not every seller will incur every category.
bullets: Commission: confirm the rate or tiered calculation and when payable.
Marketing: ask for a written schedule of included versus extra spend.
Legal and other professionals: request quotes and clarify scope.
GST: ask whether each estimate is inclusive or exclusive.

sections.heading: What the agency must explain
paragraphs: Before an agency agreement is signed, a prospective seller should receive a written appraisal, a clear commission estimate and explanation of proposed advertising expenses. Understand how cancellation, sole agency and pre-existing introductions could affect the outcome.
Do not rely on online example percentages as a quotation of Corrie's charges. His own pricing and supervising agency terms have not been published here.

sections.heading: Build a realistic budget
paragraphs: Use a range, not just one hoped-for sale price. Consider the effect of a slower sale, costs of getting a home ready, any conditional purchase and changes in interest rates. Independent legal and financial advice may be appropriate.

pages.title: Buying a House in New Zealand | Early Steps and Checks
pages.description: What to prepare before buying a New Zealand home: finance, lawyer, inspection, title, LIM, contracts and overseas-buyer rules.
pages.intro: There is no one-size-fits-all property purchase checklist. These starting points help you ask the right questions of your lender, lawyer and property professionals.

sections.heading: Confirm finance and your professional team
paragraphs: Ask your lender what borrowing amount and conditions could apply. Engage a lawyer or conveyancer before signing property documents, and discuss whether you need a building inspector, valuer or other specialist.
Allow for expenses other than the deposit, including legal fees, inspections, insurance and moving costs.

refs.label: Settled — independent buyer and seller guidance

sections.heading: Investigate the property and its legal position
paragraphs: Consider the certificate of title, LIM, council records, building condition and hazards, insurance, any tenancy or body-corporate details, and the implications of clauses in the sale and purchase agreement. Which checks matter depends on the property.
Time limits in conditional offers can be significant. Confirm them with your lawyer.

sections.heading: Understand buyer eligibility
paragraphs: If you are an overseas person, do not assume you can purchase residential land in NZ. The rules depend on specific circumstances and sometimes require consent. Consult current LINZ guidance and an independent NZ lawyer.

pages.title: Selling New Zealand Property from Overseas | Initial Guide
pages.description: Living overseas and considering selling a NZ property? Practical starting questions on communications, agency agreements, legal help and remote coordination.
pages.h1: Selling New Zealand property while overseas
pages.intro: Being overseas does not mean you should skip the same careful checks that apply to a local sale. Early planning can reduce avoidable delays and confusion.

sections.heading: Establish authority and a communication plan
paragraphs: Clarify who owns the property, who may authorise decisions and which lawyer or professional should handle the legal work. Expect an agent or lawyer to require appropriate identity and authority checks later in a secure process.
Choose a workable time zone overlap and confirm how documents will be reviewed and signed. Do not transmit passports or sensitive records through a general website enquiry.

refs.label: Settled — independent buyer and seller guidance

sections.heading: Understand the local selling process
paragraphs: A licensed professional should discuss a current evidence-based appraisal, marketing arrangements and a written agency agreement. Local inspection, photography, property access and vendor disclosures need practical coordination.
Ask how often you will receive updates and which decisions require your explicit consent.

sections.heading: Keep legal and tax questions with specialists
paragraphs: Ownership structures, residency, tax position and property history can have implications that a general website cannot decide. Obtain your own NZ legal and tax advice where needed. The existence of this guide does not mean a nationwide or cross-border service engagement has been accepted.

pages.title: Privacy and Website Enquiries | Piripi & Sons Real Estate
pages.description: How website enquiries and analytics information may be used, plus how to ask about access, correction or deletion.
pages.intro: We aim to make it clear what happens when you use this website or contact us. This is a plain-language notice for the current preliminary website and will be reviewed as services develop.

sections.heading: Information you choose to provide
paragraphs: An enquiry may include your name, email address, phone number, general reason for contacting us and the message you enter. Provide only the information necessary for an initial conversation. Please do not submit passwords, passport information, bank records, visa documents or other sensitive files.

sections.heading: How the current enquiry system works
paragraphs: The website uses Cloudflare infrastructure and an email-delivery service (Brevo) for website enquiries when direct sending is configured. The enquiry is delivered to the configured recipient inbox for follow-up. If direct delivery is not configured, the site may invite you to send an email using your own mail application.

The website also has a Google tag used for website analytics. We do not intentionally send the contents of enquiry forms, telephone numbers, email addresses or property addresses as analytics event parameters.

sections.heading: International service providers, access and enquiries
paragraphs: Some service providers may process information outside New Zealand. Enquiry details should be accessed only by people responsible for handling them. We review access and retention arrangements as the service develops.
To ask how your information is used or request access or correction, use the contact page. Any applicable legal rights and obligations take precedence over this summary.

cta.text: Contact us with a general description of your request, rather than sharing sensitive information through a public message.

pages.description: Meet Corrie Piripi, a Christchurch real estate professional with Australian property management and franchise experience, and community involvement.
pages.h1: Experience in property. Commitment to people.
pages.intro: Corrie Piripi brings a background in property management, real estate business leadership and community work to his Christchurch-based property conversations. His story reaches beyond transactions to the people and communities they affect.

sections.heading: A career shaped by property leadership
paragraphs: Corrie's professional story includes senior responsibility in Australian property management. In January 2016, Real Estate Business identified him as chief executive of Just Property Management in Bunbury, Western Australia.

That background encompasses the needs of property owners, tenants and the organisations entrusted with looking after them. In a 2022 industry interview, Coronis reported Corrie had established his own franchise business in 2021, returning to real estate after time in another industry.
These are independently reported career milestones, not claims that his earlier companies or Australian licences are his current NZ agency.

sections.heading: Practical help when a community needed it
paragraphs: An insight into Corrie's approach came during the 2016 Yarloop bushfires in Western Australia. Industry reporting described his agency working with landlords and incoming tenants to find accommodation for families displaced by the fires, alongside fundraising and other assistance.

In the same report, Corrie discussed mentoring young people and supporting local families. It illustrates a people-focused aspect of his earlier leadership that is relevant when trust and communication matter.

refs.label: Yarloop relief report, Real Estate Business

sections.heading: Community, youth and personal development
paragraphs: Corrie's public professional profile describes involvement in youth mentoring, cultural advisory work and community education programmes in Australia. It lists earlier involvement with the Bunbury Youth Consortium and local schools.

The details of historical volunteer roles come from his own professional profile and remain subject to Corrie's approval of the final biography. We have intentionally avoided publishing private family details, religious roles and personal information unrelated to his work.

refs.label: Public LinkedIn career and volunteer record

sections.heading: Australian experience, New Zealand focus
paragraphs: Corrie is now based in Christchurch. He has told us that his Australian real estate licence was transferred to a New Zealand licence under the Trans-Tasman recognition process. His exact licence class and supervising agency are being confirmed for the website.

New Zealand's Real Estate Authority provides a public register for checking current licensing. The class matters because salespeople, branch managers and agents have different responsibilities under NZ law. Clients should always know which licensed agency they are engaging.

The next chapter of Piripi & Sons Real Estate's online presence is about clear property conversations, thoughtful advice within professional authority and practical contact across Christchurch, with wider opportunities considered case by case.
